title: Watch the clouds

cards: A child lies on the grass and says, that one's a dragon. A minute later the dragon has lost its head and become a boat. A minute after that, the boat is coming apart into something with no name at all.
Somewhere along the way, the game stops, and clouds turn into weather: will it rain, do I need a jacket? But the show never stopped.
Right now, over every rooftop, shapes are forming that have never been seen before and won't be seen again. Clouds never repeat.

teach.h: A CLOUD IS AN EVENT, NOT A THING.
teach.b: First, what a cloud is. Not a thing, really. An event.
Water rises as vapor, cools, and gathers into countless tiny drops on specks of dust, and the cloud is the shape that water takes for a while before it changes again.
It's always being made and unmade at once, which is why no two are ever the same. Second, an old line that watched the same cycle.

teach.h: ALL THE RIVERS RUN INTO THE SEA.
teach.b: Ecclesiastes, in the King James words: "All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full; unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return again."
The writer saw water going round and round, and a cloud is that water on its way back up. Third, a philosopher who built a whole teaching on change.
Heraclitus, the ancient Greek thinker, is remembered, through later writers, for saying you can't step into the same river twice.
A later summary of his teaching boiled it down to two Greek words: panta rhei, everything flows. Fourth, why watching clouds is a practice of awe. It's free.
It needs no travel and no alarm.

teach.h: FREE, AND IT WON'T HOLD STILL.
teach.b: And it trains the eye on something that won't hold still for you.
The cloud you're looking at is never the same as it was a breath ago. Neither, if you look closely, is the one looking.

how: Cloud watchers lie down or sit where they can see a wide stretch of sky and follow the clouds as they form and change, without hurrying and often without naming the shapes.

games.q: you're watching a cloud that looks like a dragon. it starts to lose its shape. what does the practice ask?
o: look away and find a better one.
let it change and keep watching.
take a photo before it's gone.
games.why: the practice is watching the change itself. the cloud is never the same, and that's the point.

practice: Find a window with some sky in it, or step outside, and pick one cloud, or a patch of blue to wait in if the sky is clear. Watch one edge without naming the shape; when it becomes something else or thins away, let it.
Breathe slowly, and let your attention move as slowly as the cloud does.

wordCard.voice: Panta rhei. Heraclitus's two Greek words for everything flows, the teaching behind watching clouds that form, change and never return. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: everything flows. A later summary of Heraclitus's teaching on change.
